projects.title: Triple active bridge converter prototype
projects.summary: A SiC-based hardware prototype used to validate phase-shift modulation, soft-switching and loss models on the bench.
projects.body:
# Goal
Build a hardware platform that shows the modulation strategies from simulation working on a real converter, across the full power range.

# What it covers
- Phase-shift gate generation on a real-time controller
- Soft-switching (ZVS) checks at light and full load
- Measured efficiency compared with the loss model

> Photos and results will be added as testing progresses.

blog.title: Why phase shift controls power in a dual active bridge
blog.summary: A short, visual explanation of how the phase shift between two square waves moves power across an inductor.
blog.body:
A dual active bridge has two full bridges, one on each side of a high-frequency transformer. Each bridge produces a square wave. The only thing that separates them is a series inductance \(L\).

# The key idea
If both square waves are identical and in phase, the inductor sees no voltage and no current flows. Shift one wave by an angle \(\varphi\), and a voltage appears across the inductor for part of every half-cycle. That drives current, and with it, power.

$$P = \frac{n\,V_1 V_2}{2\pi f_s L}\;\varphi\left(1 - \frac{|\varphi|}{\pi}\right)$$

# What the equation tells us
- Power flows from the leading bridge to the lagging one.
- It peaks at \(\varphi = \pi/2\).
- A smaller \(L\) gives more power for the same shift, but higher peak current.

> In a triple active bridge the same idea applies to every pair of ports, which is why the phase shifts are coupled.
